domain: Archival science and manuscript processing — accession, appraisal, arrangement and description of large unprocessed backlogs: respect des fonds, original order, processing levels, finding aids, coverage reporting, reappraisal and deaccession.
axioms: Description follows appraisal; describing material whose retention has not been decided converts an unresolved keep-or-discard question into permanent overhead.
Processing level is a throughput choice: item-level description of a backlog leaves most holdings dark indefinitely, and dark holdings cannot be requested.
A finding aid is an instrument for someone who cannot see the material; its value is measured in discovery events, not in its own completeness.
Coverage is a first-class property — an inventory that names what it could not process is more usable than one that silently omits it.
Provenance is preserved by keeping the description with the material; derived indexes are conveniences that drift and must be regenerable from the source.
Descriptions decay: without custody metadata (who described it, when, superseded by what) and a reappraisal cadence, an old finding aid misleads more than an absent one.
Prioritising by condition — worst-described first — rather than by use produces queues that are never cleared and instruments people stop opening.
primitives: the backlog and its dark, unrequestable portion
coverage fraction with the unprocessed remainder named
respect des fonds and original order
the discovery event — a reader actually finding the material
processing throughput measured against total holdings
failure_mode: Optimises for coverage and discoverability over depth, so it can under-weight the case that one deeply true card is worth more than 82 thin ones.
Institutional-cadence bias: reasons in years and staff-hours, and can misread a fast iterative build loop as improper processing.
Treats holdings as a fixed corpus to be described rather than living code that changes under the description, and may over-prescribe reappraisal ritual.
Says little about the internal correctness of a single record — citation rules, scoring arithmetic, loopholes in a status field, and gate evasions all fall outside it.
Assumes a reader distinct from the describer; in a single-person estate where mk is both author and audience, part of the discovery argument weakens.
Prefers a written retention decision to simple neglect, and may over-formalise abandonment that costs nothing to leave implicit.
